The Mn concentration in the (Ga,Mn)N films was tuned from 0.2% to 10% by varying the growth temperature from 700°C to 590°C.
The (Ga,Mn)N films exhibited a uniform contrast in TEM analysis, with no evidence of phase separation, clusters, or nanocrystals, even at the lowest growth temperature of 590°C.

The surface morphology became more complex with decreasing growth temperature, with the formation of larger and taller hillocks, but the root-mean-square roughness remained below 3.5 nm even for the sample grown at 590°C.

The Mn concentration was reduced in the regions around threading dislocations, which can explain why the dislocations remain electrically active and can effectively shunt vertical transport across the (Ga,Mn)N layers.
X-ray diffraction patterns did not reveal any reflections corresponding to secondary phases or inclusions, confirming the single-phase nature of the (Ga,Mn)N layers.
The Curie temperature (TC) was strongly correlated with the local growth temperature across the substrate, with a 10°C variation in temperature leading to a 40% dispersion in TC.
The precise determination of TC by two different methods can serve as a tool for quantifying the spin homogeneity within the (Ga,Mn)N material.

Realizing ferromagnetism in an insulating host material like (Ga,Mn)N opens new avenues for device architectures with dissipation-less information transfer or electric-field-controlled magnetic anisotropy.

The presence of high Mn-concentrated volumes in (Ga,Mn)N is widely recognized to be the origin of the room-temperature ferromagnetism observed in some samples, and it is important to elaborate growth protocols to either enhance or eliminate these regions.

The growth temperature was found to be one of the most decisive parameters influencing the magnetic characteristics of the (Ga,Mn)N layers, allowing for fine tuning of the Mn concentration and related properties.

The authors suggest that the small variations of temperature over the substrate surface can leave a sizable imprint on the magnetic properties, which can change considerably even over millimeter distances.

The authors emphasize the necessity of performing a multi-tool characterization on the same specimens, or on as closely located specimens as possible, if there is any indication that the growth temperature may vary across the substrate.

The authors found that the Mn incorporation occurred only either for slightly-metal rich or for N-rich growth conditions, with the slightly metal-rich regime being the optimal one for obtaining a better surface morphology.

The authors note that contrary to mastering the growth conditions of related nitrides like (In,Ga)N or (Al,Ga)N, photoluminescence cannot be employed as an important characterization tool for (Ga,Mn)N due to the mid-gap location of the Mn3+ acceptor and the associated Fermi level pinning.

The authors emphasize that the growth temperature alone seems to be the most decisive parameter, and it allows for extremely fine tuning of the Mn concentration and related properties, which also applies to the incorporation of other elements required for the growth of ternary or more complex compounds.
